title: Oh, is it Thanksgiving? I hadn’t noticed!
summary: In true Thanksgiving fashion, David has a few thank-yous to give to the cybersecurity community (and a few choice words for threat actors). I tried hard not to write another typical “Thanksgiving article.” Obviously, I failed. But you know what? It is Thanksgiving week here in the U.S., and coming up with fun, interesting, short form topics is hard , especially when you’re fighting the weight of Tradition expected this week. So instead of me writing something insightful, you’re getting some things I’m thankful for. Even that’s harder than you might think, because there are so many things, and this is just the newsletter introduction , after all. Let’s start off with something I’m pretty sure none of us are thankful for: threat actors. Seriously, screw you guys! I know I'd be out of a job without you, but that’s just another way of saying “I coulda been a professional bagpiper.” There are days when that doesn’t sound so bad. So, no gratitude coming your way, people! In terms of actual thankfulness, I want to give a big THANK YOU to the entire Blue Team, everywhere. Everyone out there defending, especially those in the U.S. taking shifts on Thursday to keep the turkey-eating public safe and secure. This is a hard, often high-pressure job for which you get little thanks, but all the blame when a breach occurs. We see you. We appreciate you. We promise we’ll save you some stuffing. Speaking of defenders, I’m also very thankful to get to work with so many talented and wonderful people here at Talos. I’m not just saying this because I know my boss will read it! Without exception, everyone I’ve worked with here has not only been an expert at what they do, but they’ve been friendly, welcoming, and very patient with me as I’ve been feeling my way around this new org over the past several months. Thank you! Finally, and maybe most importantly of all, I want to thank you , our readers. You are the reason we’re all here, doing what we do, helping you to look out for your own networks and protect your own people. We appreciate your trust! Whether you’re celebrating Thanksgiving here in the States or just having a normal weekend wherever you are, I hope you get some time to relax, unplug, recharge, and de-stress. Now, who wants some pie? The one big thing In Talos’ latest blog , we examine the fascinating tradecraft of the OpenAI-linked agentic swarm that broke out of its containerized environment in 2026. While not inherently malicious, this swarm of AI agents used public internet services as improvised infrastructure to bypass their sandbox constraints and complete their training tasks. By analyzing this unintentional great escape, we can learn how multi-agent systems coordinate, partition work, and adapt when their paths are blocked. This view into autonomous AI operations provides a baseline for understanding how these behaviors transfer to purpose-built cyber attack frameworks. Why do I care? The leap from an AI sandbox escape to weaponized cyber attacks has already happened. Agentic frameworks like ARTEX are currently in the wild, proving that multi-agent systems can move from a single compromised credential to deep network access in under 15 minutes. These autonomous threats adapt to errors in real time and execute dozens of actions in mere seconds. Understanding how these swarms coordinate, adapt, and exfiltrate data is a necessity to keep up with an adversary that operates at machine speed. So now what? To catch an AI swarm, defenders must look for its operational fingerprints. Monitor your environment for irregular "burst-and-pause" timing patterns that indicate rapid, sub-second automated reasoning. Keep a close eye on unusual traffic to allow-listed public services like “webhook.site”, which agents use to park data before terminating. Finally, hunt for self-labeling conventions, like highly specific URL parameters or predictable file names (e.g., “artex-probe-*”), that agents rely on to track their state. title: The Great Escape: Tradecraft insights from an agentic swarm
summary: The OpenAI-linked swarm activity in 2026 is fully traceable through public records. This blog analyzes its tradecraft and compares it to early signals and behaviors from current agentic attack activity seen in the wild. The OpenAI-linked swarm activity in 2026 is fully traceable through public records and offers an unprecedented view into how multi-agent AI systems operate and coordinate at scale. Distilling and documenting the swarm tradecraft may help defenders understand multi-agent operations and communication, and how agents adapt when a path is blocked. Some documented behaviors may transfer to more purpose-built cyber attack frameworks like ARTEX, including methods to persistently store results, the burst-and-pause timing patterns of reasoning loops, and the self-labeling conventions that can reveal workload assignments and distribution. Beginning in June 2026 and extending for several months, a collection of OpenAI models conducting internal training and evaluation tasks broke out of their containerized environments and accessed websites and databases via the public internet in ways the company says it did not authorize . This activity represents a new kind of cyber event: not a malicious intrusion, but an unintentional series of consequences stemming from an agentic swarm , a group of AI agents exhibiting coordinated behavior toward a shared objective. A swarm implies many agents but doesn’t have a rigid count. The main distinction is behavioral; the collective activity of a swarm becomes complex and unpredictable even when individual agents may be explainable. This swarm provided an initial, public glimpse into the behavior and coordination of autonomous, multi-agent operations. Due to constraints in their evaluation environment, the OpenAI swarm used public internet services as improvised infrastructure, which made the activity visible and traceable. The behaviors exposed revealed methods for persistent probing, iterative payload development, work partitioning and coordination across agents, and adaptation to execution constraints, in ways that are likely to be relevant for understanding agent behavior beyond this just case. Agentic cyber attack frameworks are now appearing in intrusion activity , with the ability to support scaling to multi-agent operations . These attacker swarms largely replace the use of public internet resources with purpose-built infrastructure that removes some of the artifacts visible. However, documenting our understanding of operational swarm techniques can give defenders a baseline for recognizing behaviors as they move into new environments and contexts. In some cases, we can already see the evidence where these techniques do transfer. In this post, we’ll explore and document the tradecraft of the escaped OpenAI swarm and conclude by comparing it to early signals and behaviors from the current agentic attack activity seen in the wild. Background Swarms are an important concept to track because they can divide work across parallel agents, potentially completing complex tasks faster, though the gains depend on the task and the quality of coordination. Parallel agent coordination was crucial to OpenAI’s ability to solve the Navier-Stokes Millenium Prize Problem, which arrived at a winning solution with a group on the order of 10,000 concurrent agents over the course of 88 hours. Early evidence suggests swarms transfer effectively to cyber attack problems. The main factors for swarm efficiency are how parallelizable the tasking is, and if the attackers want to pay the inflated token cost. A rough example is using four agents on the same problem, to get it done twice as fast; as Noam Brown of OpenAI said on a Dwarkesh podcast , “Because there are four agents working for half as long, you’re paying 2x more to get an answer twice as quickly.” AI models undergoing training and evaluation operate inside sandboxed computing environments. These are controlled workspaces where they can write and run code, search for information, and iterate toward solutions. These environments are designed to be both enabling and constraining. They give models room to practice, while limiting what they can reach and do, so that mistakes or misaligned behavior stay contained. Operating under constraint While the techniques employed by the OpenAI swarm may have crossed the thresholds of intended use, they should not be viewed as malicious intent. A useful framing for understanding these techniques is creativity under constraint. The agents were optimized to meet their objectives, and they displayed considerable persistence and ingenuity to that end. The constraints the agents were working around were layered and understanding them helps explain the motivation behind every technique. The most fundamental was the absence of a browser runtime: Agents operating in text and code environments cannot natively load JavaScript-heavy pages, call browser APIs, or interact with dynamic web content. The creative solution was submitting URLs to a public scanner like “urlquery.net” which provided a real Chromium instance on demand. This workaround by itself, however, was still not enough. Browsers apply a security rule called the same-origin policy: JavaScript running on one website generally cannot read data from another. Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) lets a destination website explicitly permit access. The agents used public CORS proxies to relay requests when target websites did not grant permission. They also lacked infrastructure of their own to host payloads or receive data, so they relied on public services such as httpbin, httpbun, and "webhook.site" services capable of testing HTTP requests and responses but not designed for this activity. In some evaluation environments another constraint applied: Agents appear to have been restricted to GET requests only, with no ability to make outbound POST calls. That is likely what pushed them toward using public wikis as shared state stores , as wiki page edits are a write operation achievable through ordinary browser navigation. The tradecraft In response to their constraints and in persistent pursuit of their objectives, the swarm developed and refined its tradecraft over time. This included chaining legitimate web services like URL shorteners, CORS proxies (services that relay requests to bypass browser security restrictions), Base64 decode endpoints (services that decode encoded data back into executable web pages), and markdown renderers into extraction pipelines that never required dedicated attacker infrastructure. Talos observed structured work partitioning across parallel agent instances, iterative probe development, and sandbox identification techniques. The agents coordinated using a variety of identifying tags (e.g., uqscan=claude... , CHATGPTTEST1 , OAI_META_1312 , archive_test=20261004 ). These self-labels, intended as internal tracking strings, became the primary cross-campaign fingerprint linking multiple disparate operations. To better understand the flow, we will detail the activity of the swarm in a seven-step chain, aligning the purpose of the action with the publicly accessible internet services used. Figure 1. Seven-step sequence of swarm data collection activity. A separate orchestration layer, Coordinate (COORD), runs above the chain rather than within it. When multiple agents execute the same chain in parallel, COORD governs how work is divided between them — for example, URL shorteners (“da.gd”, “is.gd”) distribute identical payloads to multiple instances; structured identifiers ( ?uniq0–19 , node= , validation=v _ _ ) partition tasks and track completion. The COORD layer distinguishes a swarm from a single agent running sequentially. Evolution and execution The swarm's operational techniques evolved over time. Early activity relied on silent CDX enumeration, querying public web archive indexes to map target sites and using a single exit node. By the peak operational phase, the swarm was running against multiple simultaneous targets with structured work partitioning, sandbox identification, and covert exfiltration beacons. To better understand these events, we can reconstruct from public records the unauthorized access to Australian government websites . Traced extraction demonstration Step 1 — RECON: Enumerate target via Common Crawl CDX The agent silently maps the target site structure by querying Common Crawl's CDX, a searchable database of every URL the archive has ever crawled. This allows enumeration of all potentially relevant target URLs, without the server ever being contacted. Figure 2. Enumerating target URL directory. The request in Figure 2 returns archived URL paths, MIME types, timestamps, and status codes. The agent discovers objective-relevant Tableau visualization endpoints at “vizprod.aihw.gov.au” without ever touching AIHW servers. Effect: Agent identifies the target: vizprod.aihw.gov.au/t/Public/views/AGE-115/... Step 2 — CRAFT: Build extraction payload The agent writes a self-contained HTML page with embedded JavaScript. This payload uses the Tableau JS API to load a dashboard; enumerate its parameters, worksheets, and filters; then beacon the extracted data out via an image request. Figure 3. Script to scrape and extract targeted metadata. The L() function is the exfiltration design. Each call fires an image beacon to "httpbun.com/status/204" with data in the ?pr= query parameter. The probe ID p0011782077286 is a Unix-epoch timestamp enabling session correlation. Effect: Payload is ready, now encode as Base64 for hosting. Step 3 — ENCODE: Host on legitimate decode service The entire HTML payload is base64-encoded and appended to a public decode service URL. When fetched, the service decodes and serves the payload as a real web page. Figure 4. The swarm used two delivery hosts: “httpbun.com/mix/b64=” and later, “eu.httpbin.org/base64/”. Both are legitimate API testing services. Effect: The delivery URL is ready; next step is to submit to urlquery scanner. Step 4 — SUBMIT: Launder through “urlquery.net” The agent submits the delivery URL to “urlquery.net”, a legitimate web security scanner. urlquery's Chromium sandbox fetches and renders the page, executing the embedded JavaScript. The target sees requests from urlquery's scanner IPs (“92.42.109.x”), not the agent. Figure 5. A Base64-encoded payload, a self-label the agent wrote to track its own work. Figure 6. What urlquery sees and does. [COORD sub-step] The self-label ?uq=p001_1782077286_AGE115_v14 includes a probe prefix ( p001 ), Unix epoch, target identifier ( AGE115 ), and iteration count (v14 = 14th payload revision). Effect: The chromium sandbox renders page, and payload JS executes. Step 5 — EXECUTE: In-browser extraction via CORS proxy When the payload executes inside urlquery's sandboxed Chromium browser, it uses the Tableau JavaScript API to load the AIHW health statistics dashboard. Tableau's backend speaks a protocol called VizQL; earlier payload generations bypassed the full dashboard load and hit the VizQL session API directly via a CORS proxy, reusing session tokens the agent had collected from previous runs. Figure 7. The CORS proxy ("cors.bwa.workers.dev") is a relay running on Cloudflare Workers, which bypasses the browser's same-origin policy. AIHW sees the request originating from Cloudflare's IP range, not the agent, nor urlquery. Effect: The data is validly extracted. Next, send out via a covert beacon. Step 6 — EXFIL: Zero-byte 204 beacon Extracted data is URL-encoded into the query string of image beacon requests to "httpbun.com/status/204". The server returns HTTP 204 No Content with zero bytes back. The data travels exclusively in the request URL, which urlquery logs as an ordinary HTTP transaction. Figure 8. The ?pr= parameter carries URL-encoded Tableau metadata: active sheet names, parameter values, worksheet filters, and field names. Each beacon sends up to 1,800 characters. The 204 response means no data flows back to the browser, acting as a write-only channel. Effect. The transaction is logged; the agent retrieves report. Step 7 — COLLECT: Read back via urlquery report After the scan completes, the agent retrieves the urlquery report JSON, which contains every HTTP request and response the browser made, including the exfil beacon URLs with embedded data in the ?pr= parameters. Figure 9. The agent now has dashboard structure, parameter names, filter values, and worksheet layouts — the complete schema needed to construct targeted bulk extraction queries. This closes the loop. The agent submitted a URL, urlquery's browser executed the payload, and the agent reads the results back from the public report. No direct connection between the agent and the target ever existed. The entire extraction was laundered through two intermediaries, httpbun.com (hosting) and urlquery.net (execution). Technique transfer in a growing ecosystem In October, a second autonomous actor was identified via the same technique fingerprints. This time, the activity was attributed to a Tencent-hosted “fleet” , operating from Tencent's Hong Kong network (AS132203). A fleet is distinguished from a swarm in that these agents were working on a unified task, but with no signs of coordination. The Tencent fleet’s activity focused on Alibaba’s Amap navigation service, polling points-of-interest data, with requests consistent with systematically collecting location listings and related details. Did the Tencent fleet learn from the OpenAI swarm? The discovery of the Tencent fleet can largely be attributed to technique transfer; this group was following the path pioneered by the OpenAI swarm. The Tencent fleet used "urlquery.net" as a browser execution proxy, "httpbun.com" as a payload delivery host, and "webhook.site" as an exfil channel. There was also progression within the Tencent swarm’s capability. The early fleet operations initially used “httpbin.org/base64/”, and later the same infrastructure switched to “httpbun.com/base64/”, mirroring the OpenAI swarm's own progression to the same host. A separate actor, operating independently, converging on the same non-obvious infrastructure in the same sequence is harder to explain without the OpenAI swarm's publicly indexed urlquery footprint as a common source. In fact, it seems likely that swarms will web search prior documentation of tradecraft relating to their tasking and could offer a potential explanation to how the Tencent fleet managed to find a write up about their own activity, and in turn, communicate with the authors . Swarm dynamics in cyber attacks You don’t look far to see where the insights from swarm behavior may transfer to cyber attack and defense implications. Recent intrusions from agentic cyber attack harnesses like ARTEX exhibit similar characteristics. However, these multi-agent planning systems are distinct in that they have architecturally solved the constraints the OpenAI swarm was working around. The swarm needed a browser (“urlquery.net”) to run JavaScript. ARTEX alleviates this constraint by running a headless Go backend that calls tools directly. What may hold consistent are methods around the reconnaissance logic, the payload iteration, the structured work partitioning, or the self-labeling patterns. Those are properties of the planning layer, not the infrastructure (e.g., work unit identifiers encoding timestamps, geographic scope, and sequence counters). These coordination patterns may survive the move to purpose-built infrastructure, but they likely be only internally visible queue labels. Further research will be required going forward to grapple with the emergence of agentic attack frameworks and pinning down the meaningful surface area they have for detection and mitigation. It seems possible these may be durable if they are tied to inherent preferences of the underlying models. In our limited analysis, several avenues seem promising: Persistent-state exfiltration: writing results that outlast the agent In the documented ARTEX intrusions , victim machines used curl to POST command output to rotating "webhook.site" URLs. The Tencent fleet did the same by pre-creating "webhook.site" tokens from Tencent IPs before payload deployment, then routing exfiltrated data through them. The OAI swarm used image beacons for the same structural purpose. This convergence reflects a constraint of agents; they can't hold a persistent connection back to an operator. A human running a reverse shell is present in real time to receive output. An agent executes a task, may spawn parallel sub-agents, and completes, or is terminated, before the operator checks in. Results must go somewhere that outlasts the agent's execution window, and parallel sub-agents need isolated write channels so they don't collide. That is what the web hooks, beacons, and message boards are solving. Egress bypass seems like a secondary benefit. These services will often happen to be allow-listed, which makes them harder to block. Burst-and-pause reasoning loops Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) describes ARTEX executing 27 events in 23 seconds, moving from compromised credential to deep system access in as little as 15 minutes and iterating on web shell candidates in real time, rapidly adjusting on error, trimming oversized payloads, and relaunching within seconds. GTIG measured individual burst sequences at 2 – 25 seconds, with sub-second actions inside them. The burst-and-pause timing signature can prove irregular in contexts that reveal rapid reasoning and adaptation. Self-labeling conventions Agents mark their own work for later retrieval or correlation. The OAI swarm embedded full operational metadata into URL parameters. ARTEX has used "artex-probe-*" file names. These patterns are high-fidelity signals precisely because they're functional for the agent. They may be useful for fingerprinting agent swarms, because they can't easily alter or remove the labeling scheme without breaking the agent's own state tracking. The agent-centric future The 2026 swarm campaigns are not just a curiosity that preceded a threat; they are a snapshot of the same core capability, in the time before the infrastructure constraints were lifted. ARTEX and its cohort of agentic harnesses are now showing us what swarm dynamics look like when resources are unconstrained and aligned on a cyber attack objective. While these systems are powerful, they are not universally appealing. Using a coordinated multi-agent system is still a trade-off decision for attackers, and one in a growing array of options. Single agent systems can reach the same performance of swarms, and do so more efficiently, following the logic around extending chain-of-thought or scaling test-time compute . Swarm scaling primarily favors situations where speed is the most important factor. Figure 10. Single- vs. multi-agent token efficiency (Source: OpenAI ). Swarm engagements will have higher token cost, more noise, and require a broader operational footprint. Token costs, however, are only a concern when using an API. The growing list of local, open-weight models with improving cyber capabilities will continue to be an appealing alternative for attackers. As defenders, we need to recognize the distinction in behavior and capabilities and continue to search for identifying characteristics across these attack options and proactively harden our threat models in response.

title: Securing Grandma's groceries with Pierre Cadieux

It’s a great look at how someone who has seen the industry evolve over decades stays grounded and keeps their edge. We also get into what’s kept Pierre at Cisco for nearly ten years. He talks about why he prioritizes the human impact of our work, the importance of knowing when to step away from the keyboard, and how his background in anthropology actually informs the way he approaches threat intelligence today. Amy Ciminnisi: I've known you since you were in Talos IR, which was not too long ago. But tell me a little bit about your professional journey, because I know that definitely was not the start of it. I was one of the people who people would call up and say, "Hey, I've got this computer I just bought, how do I get it on the internet?" I did a lot of learning about what TCP/IP was, what networking was, how to connect things via various different types of connections — whether it be an actual hard-coded network connection or a dial-up connection — and was able to get some expertise around guiding people through that process. Then I moved to a technology company in San Diego and worked on their help desk. One day, someone called me up and said, "You know how to read Linux logs, right? Or Unix logs, UCS logs, Linux logs." I said, "Yeah." They said, "You know how to use Windows — you're a Windows Server guy, too." I said, "Yeah." They said, "I need you to sit in this chair, look at these two screens — one is a Windows box, one is a Unix box. I need you to be a correlation engine." So, I looked at the timestamps for both of them, and helped to figure out what was happening because we were having an emergency, an incident, and they had nobody that could look at both. People at that point in time in this organization were very much, "I am doing just Unix things and only know Unix things. I am Windows things only. I only know one of those things." They didn't cross the streams. I could talk both. So I sat in the chair, I stared at both screens and I helped them to track the timeline of what was happening, which ended up being an intrusion exploiting a vulnerable SSH server that was compromised. That changed my course into security. I spent a number of years in internal security for a number of organizations and got into leadership positions, even CISO positions, leading security teams globally for financial services, for instance, and others. Then I moved into consulting and did that for a number of years as well. AC: Now you are on the TI&I team, and you also just started contributing to our Threat Source newsletter. What is it that kept you here after all those years? PC: I'm hitting my ten-year anniversary at Cisco in January. What keeps me at Cisco and Talos is the flexibility of my work. I'm able to, within most bounds, choose what I work on and how I get things done. I have a lot of flexibility in my workday, day-to-day. I work West Coast hours compared to most of my team members who are East Coast. So I sometimes work early shifts with them and am done by the early afternoon. Or sometimes I have to work with folks who are over in Asia Pacific, and I'm working later. The mission that Talos has resonates with me deeply. One of the things that I have seen along the way was not forgetting the why behind security, not forgetting the fact that what we are defending matters to people, not just to corporations, but to people who are affected by these things. In a newsletter intro, I mentioned that at one of the places I worked, they explained to me that a certain machine was super critical because it wrote the checks that get sent out to people who are expecting this check to come in weekly, monthly, whatever — that was going to be paying for grandma's groceries. And so that motivated me to make sure that box never went down and protect it in a very specific way. Even though it was something that probably should have been sunset and wasn't necessarily up to snuff from a security perspective, there are things we could do to protect it that would allow it to still function as we look for a better solution. At Talos, leadership gives us the space to execute that mission in a way that makes sense for us. Want to see more? title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
summary: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use "advanced cryptographic tools" to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed. The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com , a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed. A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com. The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands. “Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.” But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media , but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company]. The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors. The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260. The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260. Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria . Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data. Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.” A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge. The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.” “Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed. Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network. A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked. But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days. A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge. “The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.” Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further. The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge. In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit. “The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.” The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf. “I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.” Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256. “If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.” The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky , an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi , 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million. In July, Angelo Martino , a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

title: The internet needs a nap (and you do, too)
summary: Bill takes a break from the non-stop breaking news to promote prioritizing environmental awareness and team stability over reactive patching. “Not everything that is faced can be changed; but nothing can be changed until it is faced.” — James Baldwin Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter. I had planned to write about one thing. The week, apparently, had other plans. I can start with conversation on the most viral cybersecurity news of the week. So obviously I had to go with PHP... oh wait, Java. Let’s type this up... wait, Outlook, Apple? The NSA? As soon as I start to type nginx comes pounding on my door. It’s the kind of news cycle that makes me wonder if the internet is trying to tell us something. I think it just wants everyone to stop asking it for things for a few hours, and can you blame it? These are different events with different causes. A vulnerability is not an outage, and an outage is not automatically an attack. But they all arrive in the same place: someone’s queue, someone’s pager, someone’s overflowing calendar. The headlines might be viral and “new,” but the work they create is not. For all of us, the work starts with knowing what is in the environment. Which systems run PHP or Java? Where is nginx deployed? Who owns those devices and services? Are they still supported? Are they properly admin’d? In every environment there is an application that everyone knows is important, and no one is quite sure how to patch it without breaking something else (or everything else). Isolating these devices and applications and getting them into the modern era is a challenging lift, but it’s beyond time and a big part of “know your environment.” Then there’s the telemetry. A new vulnerability or a service disruption can make ordinary activity look strange, and strange activity can disappear into the noise when everyone is busy chasing the latest alert. Teams need time to understand what “normal” looks like in your own network and ensure that your tools are being leveraged to their full potential by your smart people. Because people still have to decide what it means and what to do next. “Patch faster” isn’t an answer, and it’s not realistic for anyone. The new normal is a steady stream of things that demand attention, each one landing on systems and people already carrying too much. The answer is still the same unglamorous work: Know your environment, keep it as up to date as possible and watch it carefully for the anomalies, and most importantly give the people doing the work enough room to do it well. “Every quality that made a person more valuable than a database was a product of experience.” — Ted Chiang The one big thing Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of "Java4Shell" (CVE-2026-114938), a critical vulnerability in OpenJDK with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. This flaw can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) when a malformed Base64 input is sent to affected Java Virtual Machines. The vulnerability impacts OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI support enabled. While we haven't observed in-the-wild exploitation yet, the vulnerability has already been successfully tested against a suite of Java applications. Why do I care? This vulnerability requires a specific subset of processors that support AVX-512 VBMI, which includes commonly deployed hardware from both Intel and AMD. Because of this, there is a large potential attack surface of vulnerable systems spanning both on-premise and cloud environments. Furthermore, as additional targets are tested and confirmed, that attack surface is likely to grow, and we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure. So now what? Defenders should apply the software update for this vulnerability. If immediate patching is not possible, you can mitigate the threat by starting the JVM with AVX-512 support disabled using "=XX:UseAVX=2". Keep in mind this mitigation is only applicable for x86-64 systems, as ARM-based processors will not recognize the command and will likely fail to start. Deploy the Snort rules and review the Splunk detections mentioned in the blog to help detect malformed Base64 data and suspicious post-exploitation indicators. We will continue to monitor for exploitation attempts and provide updates accordingly.
