title: The challenge of defending against bulletproof dead drops on public blockchains
summary: The evolution of malware command-and-control (C2) infrastructure has shifted away from fragile, centralized servers and hardcoded domains toward resilient, decentralized blockchain networks that eliminate single points of failure. The evolution of malware command-and-control (C2) infrastructure has shifted away from fragile, centralized servers and hardcoded domains toward resilient, decentralized blockchain networks that eliminate single points of failure. Threat actors are leveraging immutable public ledgers such as Bitcoin transactions, EVM smart contracts via techniques like EtherHiding, TRON wallets, and Solana memo programs to store, mask, and persistently update their operational endpoints. By executing read-only remote procedure call (RPC) queries to retrieve encrypted C2 configurations directly into compromised endpoint memory, adversaries can continuously bypass traditional perimeter defenses and domain seizures. Modern cybersecurity requires a fundamental shift away from static domain blocklists toward monitoring anomalous outbound JSON-RPC traffic, analyzing endpoint memory, and treating blockchain infrastructure as an active threat communication channel. The command-and-control (C2) channel is the operational backbone of any persistent malware campaign. It is also the most fragile component. The moment an actor's C2 infrastructure is identified and reported to the hosting provider, the domain registrar, or law enforcement, the campaign's operational capability collapses. This fundamental asymmetry, where defenders need to identify only a single infrastructure link to disrupt an operation, has driven a multi-decade arms race in resilience techniques, spanning from fast flux DNS evasion to decentralized and peer-to-peer architectures. Traditional C2 infrastructure where malware beacons to a hardcoded domain or IP address is volatile by design. Security researchers or incident responders who identify the C2 address can trigger a response. The hosting provider can null-route the IP addresses and the domain registrars can suspend malicious domains under abuse policies, law enforcement can obtain court orders compelling infrastructure seizure, and threat intelligence vendors push blocklist updates that cut off the malware from its C2 links across several compromised endpoints simultaneously. This single point of failure model renders sophisticated malware families inactive once their C2 is identified and sinkholed. By redirecting malware traffic to researcher-controlled servers, researchers can not only disrupt the botnet but map the full victim community, gather forensic telemetry, and notify affected organizations. The arms race Threat actors have progressively hardened their C2 infrastructure through several evasion techniques to outpace defensive capabilities. Amongst these techniques, some of the popular approaches include the employment of domain generation algorithms (DGA), content delivery network (CDN) domain fronting, peer-to-peer (P2P) architecture, and dead drop resolvers. DGAs replace static, hardcoded server domains with dynamically generated domains. Malware programmed with a shared mathematical seed computes hundreds or thousands of pseudorandom domain names on a scheduled basis, systematically attempting to resolve each one until it establishes contact with an address registered by the threat actor. While this technique prevents defenders from neutralizing an entire operation by simply seizing or blocklisting a single domain, defenders counteracted DGAs by reverse engineering the generation algorithms, predicting future domains for proactive sinkholing, and applying machine learning models to detect algorithmically generated strings within enterprise DNS queries. The CDN domain fronting technique evolved to bypass perimeter inspection mechanisms by exploiting discrepancies between the transport and application layers of encrypted web traffic. By initiating a TLS handshake with a legitimate, reputable domain hosted on a major CDN and specifying a covert, malicious host inside the encrypted HTTP Host header, threat actors route communications through benign enterprise traffic profiles. Enterprise security tools inspecting the outer connection perceive only standard communication with a trusted global platform, effectively masking the true destination behind high reputation infrastructure. However, major cloud providers and network carriers have largely dismantled this evasion vector by standardizing routing policies and enforcing strict matching between TLS Server Name indication values and internal request headers. P2P architectures eliminate the single point of failure in a centralized server altogether by structuring infected hosts into a decentralized, self-healing mesh network. Instead of querying a primary server for instructions, compromised nodes propagate operational commands, binary updates, and collected data directly between adjacent peers using custom overlay routing protocols. This distributed topology ensures that severing dozens or even hundreds of individual endpoints leave the broader network intact and functional. Nevertheless, peer-to-peer networks suffer from inherent architectural exposure, because defenders and security researchers can enumerate the entire topology by acting as benign nodes, map peer lists, and progressively isolate the infected nodes. Dead drop resolvers establish an indirect channel by abusing established third-party web services as covert repositories for downstream infrastructure coordinates. Rather than communicating with an adversary's operational network directly, deployed malware retrieves encoded or encrypted IP addresses and domain names embedded inside public social media bios, code repository commits, or image metadata. By masking this initial discovery phase behind legitimate user activity on high-traffic consumer platforms, attackers blind simple reputation-based network defenses. Defenders eventually contain dead drop tactics by working directly with service providers to enforce aggressive account suspension, remove flagged content, and monitor automated outbound API requests from internal enterprise endpoints. Each of the above techniques still relies on some degree of centralized infrastructure that can, under the right conditions, be neutralized. The evolution of the blockchain as bulletproof hosting technique C2 configuration hosting on the blockchain eliminates the operational dependencies through embedding encrypted server addresses and URLs directly into confirmed transactions that cannot be deleted or altered by any party, preventing any single authority from taking down the records. A public blockchain is a distributed append-only ledger. Once a transaction is confirmed by the validators, it becomes a permanent, globally replicated record. The inherent architectural properties that make public blockchains attractive for financial systems translate directly into ideal characteristics for a resilient C2 configuration hosting channel. When configuration parameters such as active endpoint IP addresses and domain names or operational instructions are embedded into blockchain transactions, no single entity, cloud provider, or law enforcement agency possesses the administrative authority to delete, overwrite, or withhold that data. The ledgers are distributed globally, guaranteeing high availability and persistent access regardless of regional takedowns. Furthermore, leveraging public blockchains enables operational advantages regarding attribution and survivability. Traditional C2 mechanisms often expose the operator through payment trails, registrar records, or network traffic directed at centralized hosts. By contrast, transactions on distributed ledgers can be broadcast pseudo-anonymously through cheaper wallets and retrieving the embedded configuration data which mimics the benign blockchain queries such as public RPC API lookups or block explorer scraping. Combined with nominal transaction fees, the blockchain functions as an indestructible, globally accessible record where deployed malicious agents can reliably synchronize updates without ever exposing the core infrastructure behind them. Bitcoin blockchain adoption The adoption of the Bitcoin blockchain as a C2 configuration hosting channel began around 2016 – 2019, conceived by threat actors seeking to overcome the operational fragility of centralized hosting and vulnerable DNS registrars. Because Bitcoin transactions are permanently recorded and broadcast across nodes globally, configuration details written to the ledger become immutable, preventing law enforcement and infrastructure providers from seizing, altering, or sinkholing the underlying records. The most prominent implementation of this tradecraft emerged in September 2019 when security researchers at Trend Micro uncovered a new variant of the Glupteba botnet that used Bitcoin transactions to update its active C2 servers. Glupteba embedded a function that queried public Electrum servers for transactions linked to hardcoded script hashes controlled by the threat actors. By parsing the script, the malware extracted AES-encrypted payloads containing operational domains and fallback addresses, allowing the botnet to automatically regain connectivity whenever its active infrastructure faced defensive takedowns. Prior to Glupteba’s abuse, threat actors explored Bitcoin’s public visibility through auxiliary resolver mechanisms, notably observed in certain iterations of the Cerber ransomware and early proof-of-concept crimeware throughout 2016 and 2017. Rather than embedding direct payloads in transaction scripts, these actors monitored output transaction values, addresses, and block explorer APIs to derive seeds for pseudorandom domain generation. While these early experiments exposed the defensive blind spots of relying on public ledger lookups, the high transaction fees, block confirmation latencies, and 80-byte payload constraints of Bitcoin eventually prompted modern campaigns to migrate toward high throughput smart contract ecosystems and memo programs. Weaponization of smart contracts on public Ethereum Virtual Machine blockchains An Ethereum smart contract is an autonomous, self-executing software application deployed directly to an address on the Ethereum network. Compiled into bytecode that runs on the decentralized Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM), it is distributed across several independent nodes rather than hosted on a central server. Smart contracts operate transparently, resist blocking restrictions, and cannot be shut down or modified by any single hosting provider or authority. Smart contract architecture is more appealing to threat actors when compared to a standard transaction of a block in the blockchain. A block serves as the structural foundation of the blockchain ledger which builds verified transactions into immutable, time-stamped entries. A standard transaction represents an ephemeral event where a message is broadcasted to move funds or call an address, which may include an arbitrary payload inside the input field. Once mined, this transaction data is written permanently into blockchain history. A smart contract, by contrast, acts as a persistent entity capable of storing data that can be modified over time through subsequent transactions. Threat actors misuse this unique capability through a technique known as EtherHiding: transforming smart contracts into resilient dead drop resolvers. In the attacks, the actors deploy a smart contract holding encoded C2 domains or IP address within a contract variable. The malicious programs deployed on the compromised machines query the contract via public legitimate blockchain RPC endpoints using JSON-RPC calls such as eth_call over HTTPS and decrypt the encrypted payload received in response in the compromised machine memory and connect to the C2 infrastructure. Because eth_call simulates a contract read operation without creating an on-chain transaction, implants and scripts could retrieve live C2 addresses, leaving no transactional footprints on the ledger. The EtherHiding technique was surfaced in October 2023 , when security researchers documented how threat actors bypassed conventional domain takedowns by using Binance Smart Chain (now BNB Smart Chain) contracts as anonymous, indestructible hosting platforms. The primary cluster initially responsible for pioneering EtherHiding is the financially motivated threat actor group tracked as UNC5142 and reported by researchers in October 2025, widely associated with the ClearFake distribution campaign. ClearFake initially leveraged Cloudflare workers to deliver drive-by download lures and fake browser updates but shifted to blockchain storage when cloud vendors disrupted their operational infrastructure. Following the tactical success demonstrated by cybercriminals, state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) groups also integrated EtherHiding into targeted operations. Security researchers revealed in October 2025 that the North Korean state-sponsored threat cluster UNC5342 (linked to social engineering campaigns known as Contagious Interview) adopted EtherHiding to target developers in the cryptocurrency ecosystem. In the report, researchers disclosed that the actor UNC5342 deployed custom smart contracts on BNB Smart Chain to store second-stage payloads and active C2 endpoints for their JADESNOW and INVISIBLEFERRET malware families. They updated the configuration data more than 20 times within a few months, demonstrating how both state-sponsored adversaries and cybercriminal enterprises exploit EVM-compatible ledgers. Figure 1. A sample transaction of a smart contract hosting malicious data. TRON adoption Threat actors have increasingly embraced the TRON blockchain to construct multi-chain fallback systems that resist traditional domain seizures and infrastructure takedowns, initially reported in September 2026 . APT groups, most notably UNC5342 and Iranian state-sponsored actors, incorporate TRON as a front-line communication channel by embedding encoded routing details directly within wallet transactions. Deployed implants issue routine queries to public TRON application programming interfaces (APIs) to retrieve these transaction records, extract cryptographic keys or location pointers, and connect to secondary payload contracts hosted on platforms like BNB Smart Chain. By capitalizing on TRON's nominal transaction overhead, high processing throughput, and massive legitimate transaction volume, adversaries create an unseizable setup that forces defenders to attempt simultaneous disruptions across distinct, decentralized ecosystems to break command access. Adoption of the Solana Memo transaction On the Solana network, transactions and the Solana Program Library (SPL) memo program operate under a distinct execution model compared to EVM-based smart contracts. A Solana transaction is an atomic package containing one or more instructions executed in sequence, capable of invoking multiple independent on-chain programs within a single block confirmation. The SPL Memo Program is a native, pre-deployed utility program residing directly within the Solana runtime. Rather than managing complex state machines or maintaining custom variables, the Memo Program simply validates an arbitrary string passed to it such as UTF-8 text or Base64-encoded binary data and records it directly into the transaction’s verified execution log. Threat actors repurpose this architecture by treating the Memo Program as a lightweight, transaction-level dead drop resolver. In this technique, the actor controls standard Solana wallets and periodically broadcasts micro-value transactions that execute a call to the Memo Program. These transactions contain encrypted C2 IP addresses or staging domains. The implanted malware on the compromised endpoints is, configured with the Solana memo program ID, query public Solana JSON-RPC endpoints using standard calls like getSignaturesForAddress and getTransaction. The malware pulls the newest confirmed transaction associated with that wallet, extracts the payload from the memo instruction logs, decrypts the destination in memory, and initiates network beacons. When an operational IP or domain is sinkholed by security teams, the attacker simply broadcasts a new transaction with an updated memo payload, and the malware automatically retrieves the latest transaction on its next polling cycle without requiring binary updates on the victim machine. Solana’s technical profile presents distinct characteristics compared to earlier public blockchains when evaluated as a low-latency, resilient data distribution layer. Processing over 65,000 transactions per second with sub-second block confirmation times around 0.4 seconds, the network enables near-instant propagation of broadcast data globally, avoiding the prolonged mempool delays characteristic of Bitcoin’s seven transactions per second (TPS) or Ethereum’s 15 – 30 TPS baseline. Economically, execution fees averaging approximately U.S. $0.000025 per transaction allow several updates to be published. Threat actors are leveraging Solana memo transactions for hosting the C2 configurations that were first seen employed by the Lazarus APT group reported in March 2026. In September 2026 , Cisco Talos discovered malicious activity conducted by a suspicious North Korea-aligned threat actor UAT-12643, including the use of the Overlord RAT and implementation of a resilient C2 server discovery mechanism by using the Solana blockchain. The actor embeds encrypted C2 URLs into the Solana blockchain using the Solana Memo Program, a native Solana program that validates and permanently records arbitrary text strings in the blockchain ledger as part of a transaction. Looking ahead at defensive approach to counter bulletproof blockchain dead drops The weaponization of public blockchains ranging from legacy Bitcoin script hashes to EVM smart contracts, TRON accounts, and Solana memo fields fundamentally inverts how we counter adversary infrastructure. By turning decentralized ledgers into resilient dead drop resolvers, threat actors have removed the single points of failure that security teams traditionally rely on to dismantle operations. Standard approaches like registrar-level domain seizures, hosting takedowns, and DNS sinkholing simply don't work when the staging record lives across many immutable nodes. Enterprise defense needs to move past static indicators and focus on how endpoints interact with Web3 infrastructure. Because, resolving these dead drops relies on standard read-only Remote Procedure Call (RPC) queries, monitoring or blocking outbound traffic to public node providers like Infura, QuickNode, Tatum, and native chain endpoints could help reduce the attack surface significantly, if they aren’t required for business operations. Security teams should baseline normal developer or business activity and flag automated, high-frequency calls using methods like eth_call, getTransaction, and getSignaturesForAddress. Network defenders should inspect JSON-RPC payloads for anomalous base-encoded data and unexpected payload lengths. Also, endpoint telemetry should prioritize detecting lightweight in-memory decrypters before they can unpack and beacon out to the resolved C2 destinations. As defenders mature these detection capabilities, adversary tradecraft will inevitably shift. Talos researchers are anticipating that on-chain C2 pipelines will move towards multi-chain fallback architectures, chaining lookups across multiple cryptocurrency networks to evade single-ecosystem blocks. As commercial RPC gateways implement stricter abuse detections, attackers will likely route the RPC lookups through decentralized RPC aggregators, private transaction relayers, or zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) verification systems that obscure the querying host. Eventually, tracking this activity requires treating public ledgers not just as financial tracks, but as an active adversary communications layer.

title: UAT-12643: Suspected North Korea-aligned actor blends blockchain resilience with targeted infostealing
summary: Cisco Talos discovered malicious infrastructure associated with a financially motivated threat group we are tracking as UAT-12643. Cisco Talos discovered malicious infrastructure associated with a financially motivated threat group we are tracking as UAT-12643. The actor’s arsenal has several payloads including the Go-based Overlord remote access trojan (RAT), a Python-based infostealer internally labelled “Good Game,” and a multi-cryptocurrency clipboard hijacker. The threat actor is likely operating a campaign targeting cryptocurrency holders, gaming platform account owners, and VoIP software users based on the lure file names of the initial vectors and the payloads. The Overlord RAT implements a command-and-control (C2) resilience technique in which encrypted server URLs are embedded in Solana blockchain transaction memos. Victimology The threat actor is potentially targeting victims in Europe, according to the payload’s keyword-based file harvesting capability, which specifically targeted documents that had file names in English, French, Spanish, and Portuguese. Based on the lure themes and payload file names, the potential victim pool spans across multiple verticals. A lure financial statement decoy PDF — launched when the Good Game stealer is executed — indicates targeting finance and accounting staff. The Viber trojanized installer lure targets messaging platform users, while additional payload variants of files named microsip indicate targeting VoIP softphone operators, consistent with call-center or business telephone environments. Cryptocurrency and gaming users are also targeted by both the clipboard hijacker and the infostealer. Potential links to North Korea-aligned actors Talos assesses with low confidence that UAT-12643 is a North Korea-aligned advanced persistent threat (APT) actor based on overlaps in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) with those of the other known North Korean APT actors. In the current campaign, Talos observed that the actor is using the Overlord RAT as one of their payloads. The threat cluster called UNK_DeadDrop, likely a North Korean threat actor, had employed the Overlord RAT in their earlier campaigns as reported by the security researchers in June 2026 . The Overlord RAT variant observed in this campaign implements a blockchain C2 resilience technique with Solana blockchain transactions. This technique was first reported in March 2026 , employed by the Lazarus APT group. Although the implementation methodology differs (earlier, it was through Node.js), the technique of leveraging Solana transaction memo stayed consistent. Talos is aware that Overlord RAT and Solana blockchain hosting technique is also leveraged by other threat actors in their campaigns, as reported by external security researchers in October 2026 . Threat actor infrastructure Talos observed that the actor hosted the malicious files on a server with IP address “41[.]216[.]188[.]11”, running a Flask-based file delivery service on port 8000 with resumable byte-range download support, and serving the payload staging directory. Due to the actor’s operational security failure, the server’s root folder was exposed to the internet, and Talos’ analysis of the exposed folder showed us actor’s tool sets, and the port numbers configured on the C2 server for different services. P ort n umber Service Payload file name 8000 Flask file-drop (HTTP) Payload.exe, MyApp2.exe, HTA files 5173 Overlord RAT WebSocket C2 Ovl.exe , Client.exe 5656 Python stealer TCP C2 Ova.exe, MyApp2.exe 5959 Python stealer TCP C2 Microsip-config.exe, microsip-config1.exe The actor does not use the traditional data exfiltration approach of transferring the data to the C2 server; instead, the stolen data is exfiltrated using two different services. The actor used the discord webhook, which receives an immediate notification that contains a victim’s fingerprint and a single click download link. The stolen data archive is uploaded to “gofile[.]io” and is later accessed by the actor through the download link. We also observed the actor’s LNK generation script among the samples of the staging directory, indicating the actor’s lure creation workflow. The script accepts a payload URL and icon type (PDF, Word, or Windows Update) and generates a COM-based LNK with the spoofed and hidden execution. Figure 1. Sample Windows shortcut generation script. Initial access vectors Talos observed that the actor uses three different methods to gain initial access to victims’ environments. They have instrumented Windows shortcuts, HTA files, and XML files, so the embedded malicious instructions execute and grant initial access. In this campaign, we have not observed how the actor delivers these malicious initial vector files to victims’ machines. Weaponized LNK One of the initial access vectors is the usage of the weaponized LNK files paired with the icons spoofed from legitimate system binaries to appear as a legitimate file in the Windows Explorer. The shortcut file impersonates a PDF using the standard Windows document icon and abuses MpCmdRun.exe, Windows Defender's command line utility and the argument -DownloadFile to get the payload. Since MpCmdRun.exe is a signed Microsoft binary, the download passes application allowlisting controls transparently. The downloaded payload will be saved as RuntimeBroker.exe to blend into process inventories, and the console window is minimized with no visible trace. Figure 2. Embedded command line in a sample LNK. Another shortcut file applies the same PDF disguise through a double-extension file name and the Microsoft Edge PDF icon and uses certutil -urlcache –f, a one-liner download command that operates under the guise of a certificate cache update. Both shortcuts were built on the same machine (win-8oa3ccqae4d). Figure 3. Embedded command line in a sample LNK. HTA dropper Talos observed that the actor has weaponized the JavaScript HTML Application (HTA) file to gain initial access. The weaponized HTA is executed by mshta.exe and the JavaScript in the HTA uses “MSXML2.ServerXMLHTTP” to fetch the payload as raw binary and “ADODB.Stream” to write it to %TEMP%\s.exe, then executes it stealthily by hiding the execution window. Figure 4. Sample HTA file. MSBuild living-off-the-land binary (LOLBin) The actor has also weaponized a standard MSBuild XML project file “dl.xml” by including an inline C# CodeTaskFactory task. When the XML file is executed via msbuild.exe, it compiles and executes the C# code in memory, and no intermediate executable is written to disk for the downloader stage. The download uses a spoofed Microsoft BITS/7.8 User-Agent string, impersonating the Windows Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) used by Windows Update, Microsoft Defender and many third-party updaters, so the request blends in with routine background download traffic. Figure 5. Sample malicious MSBuild project XML file. Analysis of Overlord RAT The Overlord RAT variant utilized by UAT-12643 in this campaign is a modular Windows RAT compiled from Go source code. The defense evasion and anti-analysis techniques implemented include the detection of in-memory execution to suppress forensic artifacts when running in sandboxes and a “kill flag” mechanism that triggers a kernel-level Blue Screen of Death (BSoD), making the process effectively unremovable without triggering a full system crash. The RAT first verifies that the current process is running with administrative privilege. It then acquires SeDebugPrivilege for the current process. With that privilege held, it calls a native NT kernel API (NtSetInformationProcess) directly, bypassing the documented Win32 API layer entirely, to set the ProcessBreakOnTermination information class on the current process handle to value 1, which indicates the kernel will handle the process as critical to system operation. With these settings, the operating system treats the process the same way as the core Windows system processes. When a user or a security tool attempt to forcibly terminate the process, the kernel does not allow it to exit cleanly. Instead, it immediately halts the entire operating system and triggers a BSoD with the stop code CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED. Figure 6. Snippet of Overlord RAT function that triggers BSoD. For persistence, the RAT employs two approaches. The primary approach is through a registry autorun entry under the current user's hive, with a randomized value name pointing to the RAT binary located in the Network folder of the local user profile application data folder. The secondary approach is a pre-boot persistence via the Windows Recovery Environment OEM script path. It first removes any previous version of itself and then sets up the OEM environment directly under %TARGETOSDRIVE%\Recovery\OEM\. This folder is the location that the Windows Recovery Environment accesses when performing a "Reset this PC" operation. By placing files here, anything registered in this directory gets executed inside WinRE before the operating system is restored. Once the directory is set, the RAT generates a random 20-character file name for its payload file. Each character is picked individually at random from a fixed character set, meaning every installation produces a uniquely named file. With a random name chosen, it writes the RAT's own executable binary into the OEM directory as that payload file. It then constructs the shell command that WinRE will use to launch the payload and wraps it into Windows batch script with the .bat extension. cmd.exe /c start %TARGETOSDRIVE%\Recovery\OEM\"random_stub_name" The use of %TARGETOSDRIVE% is significant, as this environment variable only exists and resolves correctly inside the WinRE pre-boot environment, not in normal Windows. This means the command is specifically crafted to work at recovery time, not during a regular session. Before modifying any system configuration, it backs up the existing WinRE reset configuration file. Finally, it modifies the ResetConfig.xml file that governs what WinRE does during a reset. If no config file exists yet, it creates one from scratch; if one already exists, it patches it to append the malicious batch scripts as registered OEM tasks. From this point forward, whenever the victim triggers "Reset this PC" whether from within Windows Settings or from the recovery boot menu, Windows Recovery Environment will execute the RAT's payload before restoring the operating system, ensuring the implant survives a full system reset. Figure 7. Snippet of Overlord RAT function configuring the malicious script in WinRE location. Analysis of the RAT’s binary showed a complete command surface with 35 commands, each corresponding to a distinct capability delivered over the C2 channel. These commands belong to several remote administration capability categories as described in the table below: Category Capabilities Surveillance Captures keystroke using GetAsyncKeyState , Webcam streaming, microphone and desktop audio capture and desktop screen capture. File system Directory listing and creation, file read, write, delete , copy, move, perform recursive search, upload, download, and compression ta sks. Process control Process enumeration and termination. Script execution Execute arbitrary command and script with real-time console output streaming back to C2. Lateral Movement Establishes Reverse SOCKS proxy tunnel that routes operator TCP traffic through the victim network, enabling access to internal hosts unreachable from the public internet. Plugin delivery HTTP-based plugin downloads with reflective DLL injection at runtime where new capabilities are loaded entirely in memory with no binary update or written to the disk. Overlord’s Solana blockchain C2 URL hosting The RAT implements a resilient C2 server discovery mechanism by using the Solana blockchain. The actor embeds encrypted C2 URLs into the Solana blockchain using the Solana Memo Program, a native Solana program that validates and permanently records arbitrary text strings in the blockchain ledger as part of a transaction. Any Solana wallet can include a memo instruction in a transaction of up to 566 bytes of arbitrary data to the permanent, globally replicated transaction record. Figure 8. The Snippet of Overlord RAT function queries the Solana Memo address. A threat actor can post one such transaction from a controlled wallet address whenever the C2 server address needs to be updated. Every deployed RAT picks up the update on its next discovery cycle without any redeployment or reconfiguration. This is achieved by first retrieving the transaction history for the actor-controlled wallet using the Solana getSignatures JSON-RPC method which receives a chronologically ordered list of transaction signatures with the newest transaction first. For each signature it fetches the full transaction via getTransaction with jsonParsed encoding, which instructs the RPC node to decode every instruction data field into structured JSON response. The RAT module then walks every instruction in the parsed transaction looking for one whose data string is exactly 43 characters in length. The 43-character length is the fixed string length produced when a Base58-encoded WebSocket URL is AES-256 encrypted. Any instruction whose data field is a different length will be skipped, including legitimate Memo transactions from other users and all other Solana program instructions. Only instructions matching this precise length signature are treated as C2 memos. Figure 9. RPC response format for the getTransaction request. Good Game stealer The Good Game stealer payload Talos observed in the arsenal of UAT-12643 is a publicly available Python-based infostealer developed under the label " Good Game ( version 1.1.2)” by CirqueiraDev . The actor of this campaign is not the developer, and the malware is distributed as a self-contained Windows executable produced by packaging a Python 3.12.0 code with PyInstaller. Its architecture is split between two cooperating bytecode modules. The “final_build.pyc” acts as the launcher, decoy interface, and reverse-shell client, while “kora.pyc” contains the full data-harvesting stealer logic. Good Game’s anti-analysis and evasion The malware employs evasion techniques at every stage of execution, beginning the moment the process starts. The launcher immediately retrieves the console window handle via GetConsoleWindow() and calls ShowWindow() to hide the terminal window. A fully functional Notepad-style graphical user interface (GUI) is rendered in the foreground via tkinter, a Python’s standard, built-in library used for creating GUIs while all malicious threads run as daemon threads behind it. Before the stealer module begins with any data collection, it runs three sequential execution checks. First, it confirms the host operating system is Windows by checking platform.system(); the stealer aborts silently on Linux or macOS. Second, it verifies network connectivity by performing an HTTP GET request to Google, and if the request fails, the stealer exits and records the failure reason in a file named “skipped" in the temporary directory. Third, and most significantly, it runs sandbox detection checks in five steps. It checks for the presence of libraries including sbiedll.dll, api_log.dll, vmcheck.dll, wpespy.dll, cmdvrt64.dll, avghookx.dll, snxhk.dll, and guard32.dll. The MAC address check extracts the host's network adapter hardware address via the getmac module and compares it against known OUI prefixes assigned to virtualization vendors: VMware (00:05:69, 00:0c:29, 00:50:56), VirtualBox (08:00:27), Hyper-V (00:15:5d), Xen (00:16:3e), and Parallels (00:1c:42). The hardware memory check queries GlobalMemoryStatusEx through a ctypes MEMORYSTATUS structure and flags machines with less than two gigabytes of physical RAM as sandbox environments. The boot-time check uses psutil.boot_time() to compute system uptime and treats an uptime of fewer than five minutes as indicative of a freshly provisioned analysis VM. Finally, the Wine emulation check probes for the presence of “C:\windows\system32\wineboot.exe” to detect Windows API compatibility layers. If any single check triggers, the stealer exits silently, leaving no harvested data and minimal trace. The decoy URL mechanism of the stealer adds a further layer of camouflage. It opens a PDF-hosted document in the victim's default browser exactly once per machine and computes an MD5 hash of the URL and stores a flag file named “url_opened_ .flag” in the temporary directory of the victim machine. On all subsequent executions, the lure URL is not re-opened, preventing repeated suspicious browser launches that would alert the victim. Figure 10. Decoy PDF opened by Good Game stealer in victim’s browser. Persistence established by Good Game The malware establishes persistence through two independent mechanisms on Windows, ensuring the implant survives reboots regardless of which pathway is disrupted. The primary method is a registry autorun by opening the key HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run using winreg.KEY_SET_VALUE” and writes the absolute filesystem path of the running executable under the value name Zoipers , causing the binary to be launched automatically at every subsequent user logon without requiring elevated privileges. The secondary persistence mechanism is executed from within the stealer module of kora.pyc. The stealer copies the running executable into the Windows Startup folder at %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\ using shutil.copy(). Beyond simple re-execution persistence, the stealer also temporarily disables the Windows Task Manager during its active operation. It calls advapi32.RegCreateKeyExW directly through ctypes against the key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System and sets a DWORD value DisableTaskMgr=1 via RegSetValueExW. After the data exfiltration completes successfully, the stealer restores the value to zero ( DisableTaskMgr=0 ), reducing the probability that the victim will notice the restriction. Good Game stealer functionalities The stealer's most extensive capability targets 23 Chromium-family and Firefox-based browser variants, covering Google Chrome across all distribution channels, Microsoft Edge, Opera, Opera GX, Brave, Vivaldi, Yandex Browser and all its regional variants, Amigo, Torch, Kometa, Orbitum, CentBrowser, 7Star, Sputnik, Epic Privacy Browser, Uran, and Iridium. The stealer scans LevelDB stores across Discord clients and over 19 Chromium-based browsers for authentication tokens using two regex patterns one for plain-text tokens and one for tokens encrypted with the “dQw4w9WgXcQ:” prefix introduced in newer Discord versions. It decrypts the stolen token via the browser's extracted master key, then validates each recovered token against the Discord API to build a complete account profile covering username, display name, user ID, email, phone number, Nitro subscription tier, linked payment methods, gift codes, and multi-factor authentication (MFA) status. The stealer additionally extracts ROBLOSECURITY cookies from browser databases, validating each against the Roblox authentication API to confirm active sessions and retrieve the associated account details. A full system profile is assembled covering hostname, username, hardware specifications, OS details, network interfaces, and public IP geolocation metadata queried from ipwhois.app, serialized to system_infos.txt in the archive root. The stealer also captures a full-monitor screenshot and a single webcam frame, both saved as PNGs and added to the archive before the temporary files are deleted and terminated. The stealer then harvests session data from 21 cryptocurrency wallets including Exodus, Electrum, Ledger Live, Trezor Suite, Atomic Wallet, Trust Wallet, Coinbase, and Binance, as well as four gaming platform launchers (Steam, Riot Games, Epic Games, and Rockstar Games). Beyond structured credential databases, the stealer conducts a targeted sweep of the victim's personal file system across the folders Desktop, Downloads, Documents, Pictures, Videos, OneDrive root, and the Windows Recent Items folder at %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Recent. The sweep applies to two independent filters that a file must satisfy simultaneously before it is collected. The first filter is an extension allowlist covering 45 file types spanning different categories mentioned in the table below: File types File extension Plain text and configuration formats .txt, .log, . ini , . json , .xml, .csv, .md, .rtf, . cfg , .conf Image formats . png , .jpg, .jpeg, .bmp, .gif, .tiff, . svg , . webp Document formats .pdf, .doc, .docx, . xls , .xlsx, .ppt, .pptx, . odt , . ods , . odp archive formats .zip, . rar , .7z, .tar, . gz , .bz2 video and audio formats .mp4, .avi, . mkv , .mov, . wmv , .flv,.mp3, .wav, . aac , . flac , . ogg The second filter is a keyword allowlist of four languages English, French, Spanish, and Portuguese that must match the file's base name exactly. The keyword list is designed to maximize overlap with the types of sensitive documents that cryptocurrency users, online gamers, and financially active individuals are likely to store on their desktops or in their documents folders. It covers two-factor authentication backup codes, mnemonic seed phrases, cryptocurrency wallet application names, generic password file naming conventions, banking and payment terms, private key and recovery phrase labels, Discord authentication tokens, Telegram session identifiers, and generic high-value labels such as secret, vault, backup, admin, and root. Files that satisfy both the extension and keyword filters are written into the archive in the temporary directory, with each file name suffixed by a randomly generated four-digit number before the extension. Figure 11. Targeted files search and exfiltration program for Good Game stealer. Data exfiltration mechanism of Good Game stealer All harvested data is written progressively into a single ZIP file. The ZIP file object is opened with ZIP_DEFLATED compression in the system temporary directory. The archive file name uses the prefix “SK_”, followed by eight randomly generated characters, creating a unique identifier per victim and making the archive harder to identify by name alone. The ZIP is structured into named subdirectories such as Screenshot/, Webcam/, Session Files/Wallets/, Session Files/Game Launchers/, Session Files/Apps/Telegram/, and Interesting Files/ alongside flat files in the root for system information and antivirus enumeration results. Browser-derived outputs are labelled with a count suffix such as Passwords (N).txt, where N reflects the number of credentials recovered from that browser, enabling the actor to prioritize. Once all stealer modules have been completed, the closed archive is uploaded to hxxps[:]//upload[.]gofile[.]io/uploadFile using an HTTP POST request. The server returns a JSON response containing a direct download link to the uploaded archive. Figure 12. Snippet of Good Game stealer exfiltration function. With the GoFile download URL in hand, the stealer constructs a Discord webhook notification and POSTs it to the hardcoded webhook endpoint. The notification takes the form of a Discord message containing the victim's hostname, username, machine architecture, operating system version, and OS release label providing the operator with an immediate preview of the victim's machine profile without needing to download the archive first. After the webhook POST completes, the stealer calls its cleanup routine to delete the local ZIP archive and all temporary intermediate files including the screenshot PNG and webcam PNG from the temporary directory. Figure 13. Snippet of Good Game that POSTs reconnaissance data to Discord Webhook. Clipboard hijacker targets multi-cryptocurrency wallet addresses The clipboard hijacker Talos identified in the actor’s toolset is a compact Windows x64 executable written in C++. It has no network component or C2 communication protocol; instead, the actor configuration is compiled directly into the binary as XOR-encrypted wallet addresses in the binary data section. Upon execution, the binary dynamically resolves the API function addresses and creates a global mutex “UuuRjinBZPBMIjnc”. Then it retrieves the machine name and searches for the substrings including VBOX, VMWARE, QEMU, and SANDBOX. Persistence is established by copying the binary to %APPDATA%\MsgEdgeUpdate.exe with FILE_ATTRIBUTE_HIDDEN and FILE_ATTRIBUTE_SYSTEM attributes applied, then adding it under user hive’s Run registry key with value named “MsgEdgeUpdate”, spoofing the appearance of a legitimate Microsoft Edge updater process. The hijacker polls the Windows clipboard every 500 milliseconds in an infinite loop, applying address-format fingerprinting to detect the copied cryptocurrency. All clipboard APIs are resolved dynamically through user32.dll. On detection, the corresponding attacker wallet address is XOR-decrypted from the data section and overwrites the original wallet address in the victim machine clipboard. Coverage The following ClamAV signatures detect and block this threat: Win.Trojan.OverlordRAT-10060615-0 Ps1.Trojan.LNKBuilder-10060627-0 Win.Trojan.OverlordRAT2-10060616-0 Win.Infostealer.GoodGame-10060617-0 Win.Infostealer.PyStealerDeps-10060618-0 Py.Infostealer.GoodGame-10060619-0 Py.Trojan.GoodGameLoader-10060620-0 Win.Trojan.WalletClipper-10060621-0 Win.Downloader.LNKMpCmdRun-10060622-0 Win.Downloader.LNKCertutil-10060623-0 Win.Trojan.LNKVideosExe-10060624-0 Html.Downloader.HTAStager-10060656-1 Xml.Downloader.MSBuildInline2-10060657-0 The following Snort2 and Snort3 Snort Rules (SIDs) detect and block this threat: Snort2: 1:67491, 1:67490 Snort3: 7:75, 7:74 Indicators of compromise (IOCs) IOCs for this research can be found at our GitHub repository here .

title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
summary: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content. At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely , a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC , CNN , Equifax , Ledger and Zoom , was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content. The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge. According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI , on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s. Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “ DarkSword ” and “ Coruna ,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data. “The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote . “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.” Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.” “We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.” Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content. One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files. Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds . Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing. “So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.” Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “ Content Security Policies ” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons. “With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.” How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload. Image: blog.report-uri.com. The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja , which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records. Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West. “Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.” Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website. Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You? Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

title: CVE-2026-114938: Critical vulnerability in OpenJDK Java
summary: Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of a critical vulnerability in OpenJDK Java (CVE-2026-114938), dubbed “Java4Shell,” with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 that may lead to unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Update 11/18/2026: Cisco has released a security advisory on products potentially affected by this vulnerability. Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of a critical vulnerability in OpenJDK Java (CVE-2026-114938), dubbed “Java4Shell,” with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 that may lead to unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). This vulnerability can be triggered by sending a malformed Base64 input to affected JVMs, which can result in RCE. Details This vulnerability affects OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled. These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed. This vulnerability does require a specific subset of processors that support AVX-512 VBMI; these include commonly deployed processors from both Intel and AMD, resulting in a large potential attack surface of vulnerable systems, including both on-premise and cloud environments. Cisco Talos would like to thank Calif.io for sharing the details of the vulnerability in advance of public disclosure . Observed exploitation Talos has not observed in-the-wild exploitation of this vulnerability yet. However, we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure. Talos will continue to monitor for exploitation attempts and will provide updates accordingly. Recommendations and guidance Talos recommends applying the software update for this vulnerability. If immediate patching is not possible, other mitigations can be implemented in the interim. The primary mitigation is starting the JVM with AVX-512 support disabled. This can be done by starting the application with “=XX:UseAVX=2”. Note that this is only applicable for x86-64 systems, as ARM-based processors will not recognize the command, likely resulting in failure to start. Cisco is following its well-established process to evaluate its products and customers are strongly advised to refer to Cisco’s security advisory on potentially affected products. Customers should reach out to their sales teams with specific questions. Coverage SNORT® SIDs covering this vulnerability for subscribers: Snort2: 1:67502 - 1:67513 Snort3: 1:301754, 1:67502 - 1:67513 Free community rules are live through our Community Ruleset . These rules detect malformed Base64 data in specific HTTP request fields associated with the vulnerability. This vulnerability is implementation specific. Talos made every effort to identify as many common vulnerable applications as possible and cover potential attack vectors in those applications. Splunk customers can refer to Splunk’s ES Content Updates (ESCU) pre-packaged security content for detections against high-profile vulnerabilities. Existing detections from Splunk cover suspicious indicators such as heavily encoded content , and post-exploitation scenarios such as arbitrary command execution or processes and web or application servers spawning shells .

title: ARTEX and beyond: AI-enabled penetration testing platforms
summary: AI-enabled penetration testing and red team frameworks can automate and chain reconnaissance, vulnerability testing, and follow-on actions, lowering the skill threshold for attackers and accelerating intrusions when the tools are misused. Cisco Talos is tracking the growing in-the-wild usage of AI-enabled penetration testing frameworks. AI-enabled penetration testing and red team frameworks can automate and chain reconnaissance, vulnerability testing, and follow-on actions, lowering the skill threshold for attackers and accelerating intrusions when the tools are misused. Talos has seen full automation of the attack chain by these frameworks, which not only use free and open-source tools, like nmap and nuclei, but also take advantage of internet mapping services like Censys and Shodan, CAPTCHA bypass services, credential leak management services, residential proxies, and even hash cracking services. This is the case of Hephaestus, which we mentioned in our previous report . Although these frameworks all have the same purpose, they come in different flavors. Some, like Hephaestus, are command line tools which can be deployed with a single script on a VPS and are completely controllable via Telegram. PentAGI has a web interface to monitor the agent activity with a full attack chain graph design and monitoring. Talos found more than 700 instances of currently reachable PentAGI instances on the internet. HexStrike AI integrates with many different clients like Claude Code, VS Code, or any other client that supports MCP. One such framework making waves, ARTEX, has enabled threat actors to scale offensive operations, compressing work that may have previously taken skilled teams hours or days into activity that can unfold at machine speed. Talos’ analysis of ARTEX-associated IP addresses identified a diverse set of tools concurrently present on that infrastructure, reinforcing ARTEX’s role in a broader and varied threat environment. AI-enabled frameworks: A new reality Before we delve into ARTEX, it is clear that these frameworks are the new reality. Their evolution will most likely include autonomous lateral movement followed by data identification and exfiltration. The precursor of this can already be seen in the victim prioritization of the Volta Infostealer, described in detail in this Talos report . It is highly likely that future attack chains involving these frameworks will culminate in data exfiltration and ransomware activation, all being done autonomously by one of these frameworks. Such evolutions present new challenges to defenders: It reduces the time it takes to detect a compromise without any known indicators of compromise (IOCs). We provide guidance to help overcome this challenge in the Recommendations section. After malicious activity is identified, it is crucial to contain the incidents. These frameworks work at speeds that can make it impossible for human operators to identify, assess and react in time to disrupt the attack. These frameworks make mitigation and containment, along with a battle-tested cybersecurity incident response plan, imperative for organizations' resiliency. Defenders using AI can be a force multiplier to provide much-needed improvements, both in the speed and scale of response to such attacks. ARTEX ARTEX is an AI-enabled penetration testing framework developed under the pseudonym Autumn-27 and published on GitHub in July 2026. An operator gives it a target and objective, a planner agent breaks the objective into tasks, worker agents perform them using security tools, and the framework records assets, findings, and progress in a shared graph. ARTEX can use different large language models (LLMs) and requires relatively little operator input after a task begins. It was designed for authorized security testing, but recent public reporting documented its use in both criminal and targeted intrusion campaigns within weeks of its release. It is important to note that ARTEX is not natively bundled with any traditional command-and-control (C2) framework, though the Model Context Protocol (MCP) extensibility layer means any compatible tool server can be added by an operator. This explains why we have observed multiple instances of ARTEX being deployed alongside tools such as VShell, GoPhish, and AdaptixC2. Threat actors leveraging ARTEX in offensive campaigns Multiple threat actors with distinct motives and tradecraft have been associated with ARTEX activity; its release as open-source software, followed by the continued availability of forks and copies, almost certainly facilitated adoption across different actor groups. Public reporting (referenced below) and Talos observations indicate ARTEX is largely used by financially motivated cybercriminals and threat actors with a China nexus. Observed ARTEX campaigns range from opportunistic scanning and credential theft to targeted intrusions and supply chain activity, with targets spanning financial services, cryptocurrency, government, telecommunications, defense, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, and technology organizations across multiple regions. Reported outcomes vary from unsuccessful attempts to confirmed compromise and data exfiltration. Reported campaigns: VAPOR PANDA : CrowdStrike attributed an espionage campaign (beginning Oct. 17, 2026) leveraging ARTEX to China-nexus actor VAPOR PANDA. The actor used ARTEX against more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries, with targets that included government ministries, telecommunications providers, and organizations in the defense, pharmaceutical, semiconductor, nuclear, and financial sectors. CrowdStrike confirmed post-compromise activity at nine organizations and reported additional credential-scanning and password-spraying activity against at least 12 others. Storm-0940 : Microsoft attributed ARTEX-driven activity to Storm-0940, who they assess is a “China-state aligned actor”. Following the compromise of ConnectWise application credentials, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate sign-in attempts against more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 tenants, with follow-on activity involving Microsoft Graph, application credentials, and privilege changes. Storm-3358 : Microsoft also reported financially motivated Storm-3358 activity targeting financial organizations, primarily in Southeast Asia, and describes the cluster as Cambodia-based. Its ARTEX activity included exploitation of public-facing systems and deployment of remote access trojans (RATs). Cisco’s observations for this cluster are in line with Microsoft’s findings. We found IP addresses associated with this cluster conducted asset scanning in October 2026. Unidentified Chinese-speaking threat group : CrowdStrike reported an unattributed campaign against South Korean financial organizations that resulted in data exfiltration; it assessed with moderate confidence that the actor was Chinese-speaking and financially motivated. Talos separately analyzed actor-associated directories used in these attacks and found ARTEX-related artifacts, including directory listings and prompt history references. The archive did not contain the ARTEX executable or source tree, so these artifacts support an association with an ARTEX environment but do not, by themselves, prove that the complete framework was present or used in a successful attack. Unidentified criminal threat actors : Check Point Research documented additional criminal operators pursuing goals that included stealing code-signing certificates and gaming-account credentials and attempting cryptocurrency theft. Unattributed ARTEX-associated activity: Microsoft reported agents using ARTEX to search public GitHub repositories for exposed credentials, including application credentials and AI service API keys, and then use discovered secrets for follow-on activity. In one case, the agent moved from searching GitHub to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault within five minutes. Datadog separately observed ARTEX activity in AWS environments involving compromised long-term access keys and public Cognito user pools. The activity included searching cloud logs for financial information and secrets, registering accounts, collecting tokens, and attempting cloud resource enumeration. Datadog did not attribute these observations to a named actor. Finally, Dosu disclosed a separate ARTEX-related incident in which an attacker progressed from account creation and an authorization flaw to access involving integrations, CI, a database, and cloud systems. Dosu reported that the attacker generated more than 80,000 requests in 90 minutes. Observed tactics, techniques, and procedures Across campaigns, ARTEX has served as an orchestration layer for rapid, parallel reconnaissance and intrusion activity, enabling actors to turn exposed credentials or application weaknesses into broader access, persistence, and data theft. Operators typically set the objective and provided limited direction, while agents adapted their approach to the target. The resulting behaviors vary by campaign and should not be treated as a single fixed playbook. Planning and reconnaissance: ARTEX operators provide objectives and may assign tasks across multiple targets; its planner and worker agents can then conduct activities in parallel and record results for subsequent tasks. Check Point’s review of operator consoles found that agents often worked with little interaction after the initial goals were set, while VAPOR PANDA was seen steering agents at selected decision points. Reported reconnaissance includes scanning public-facing applications and services, testing authentication flows, enumerating cloud resources, and searching public code repositories for exposed secrets. ARTEX activity may generate varied requests and rapid retries, but tool signatures and user agents can change and should be treated as supporting indicators rather than definitive attribution. Initial access and exploitation : Reported initial access methods in ARTEX campaigns include password spraying, exposed or stolen credentials, and exploitation of application and authorization flaws. Observed weaknesses that were exploited in these attacks include weak or hardcoded administrative credentials, missing API authentication, insecure direct object references, command injection or template injection vulnerabilities, anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery weaknesses, and lack of defenses against privilege escalation. These observed tactics support that ARTEX can automate the discovery and use of weaknesses in web applications and identity systems, but the specific techniques depend on the target and campaign. Credential access and cloud abuse : Several ARTEX attacks leveraged the discovery or misuse of credentials as a bridge from an initial foothold to cloud resources and downstream systems. For example, agents were observed searching public GitHub repositories for credentials and API keys, then using exposed secrets for follow-on activity, including access to Azure Key Vault. Another campaign included AWS activity involving anonymous S3 requests, compromised long-term access keys, CloudWatch log searches, and public Cognito user pools. In the Cognito activity, agents registered accounts, collected tokens, and attempted AWS resource enumeration. Microsoft’s Storm-0940 reporting describes compromised application credentials being used to access downstream Microsoft 365 tenants and conduct follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph. Privilege escalation, persistence, and lateral movement : Observed follow-on behaviors include changes to application permissions, token or credential abuse, access to privileged accounts, and deployment of web shells or RATs. CrowdStrike describes VAPOR PANDA using historical authentication material to forge an administrator token, read mailboxes, and reach an internal network using recovered VPN information. It also reports endpoint-security discovery, web-shell deployment, and use of the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor in other parts of the campaign. Microsoft reports Storm-3358 deploying WISP, VShell, and AdaptixC2 for persistence and lateral movement. Of note, these actions are actor-specific examples rather than default ARTEX behavior. Collection, exfiltration, and impact : As detailed in the above campaigns, threat actor objectives include credential and data theft, financial gain, and supply chain compromise. Observed impacts range from access to cloud secrets and mailbox data to the use of compromised applications to reach connected environments. Concurrent tooling observed on ARTEX-associated infrastructure ARTEX is an agentic penetration testing platform that can direct and coordinate other security tools as part of its workflows. Talos identified more than 2,500 ARTEX-associated C2 IP addresses, then analyzed the tools observed on those systems and compared their observation periods with ARTEX. The tools below are ordered from most to least frequently observed during overlapping periods. Although co-occurrence does not confirm with certainty that ARTEX invoked each tool or that all were operated by the same actor, this list can help prioritize defenses against potential ARTEX-associated activity. ScopeWeaver : A localized derivative of ARTEX, rebranded and translated into English and Korean AntiFox : Delivery-enhanced version of ARTEX, reproduction captured in place and provides easy-to-know kill chain findings CyberStrikeAI : An AI-based security testing platform that coordinates agents and external tools for automated assessments PentAGI : An open-source, self-hosted platform that uses multiple AI agents to plan and conduct penetration tests in an isolated environment ScopeSentry : An asset discovery and vulnerability scanning platform developed by the same pseudonymous author as ARTEX VShell : A cross-platform C2 framework primarily used for post-exploitation activities and often compared to Cobalt Strike, given overlapping offensive capabilities Nessus : Tenable’s vulnerability assessment scanner, used to identify vulnerabilities and configuration issues across systems and networks Interactsh : ProjectDiscovery’s open-source tool for detecting out-of-band interactions that can reveal vulnerabilities triggered by external callbacks Acunetix : An automated web application security scanner that crawls websites and tests for vulnerabilities Fscan : An open-source internal network security scanner Net Proxy Server (NPS) : An open-source proxy and tunneling server designed to provide access to services behind a network boundary AdaptixC2 : An extensible C2 and post-exploitation framework intended for authorized red team assessments Mimikatz : An open-source post-exploitation tool used to extract plaintext passwords, hashes, PIN codes, and Kerberos tickets from Windows memory Cobalt Strike : Fortra’s commercial adversary-simulation and red team platform, which includes capabilities for post-exploitation activity Gophish : An open-source platform for conducting and tracking phishing simulations Chisel : An open-source TCP/UDP tunneling tool that transports connections over HTTP and secures them with SSH; it can also relay traffic through proxy or reverse-tunnel configurations Recommendations For frameworks that pursue operator-defined objectives through adaptable workflows and supporting tools, associated activity can vary by target and operator. Defenders should focus on fundamentals that limit the speed and scale of attacks, reduce exposure, protect credentials and cloud identities, and quickly detect suspicious activity. Monitor for rapid, unusual activity : Correlate authentication, cloud API, and endpoint logs to detect high-volume requests, unfamiliar applications, token use, and privilege changes. Harden public-facing systems : Patch promptly, remove default credentials, and test authentication and authorization controls. Defend against credential attacks : Require multi-factor authentication (MFA) for remote and privileged access; apply rate limits and alert on password-spraying patterns. Harden endpoint detection : Enable endpoint detection and response (EDR) tamper protection and sensor health monitoring, alert on service or configuration changes, and retain independent telemetry to investigate attempted defense evasion, as ARTEX has demonstrated EDR bypass capabilities. Protect exposed secrets : Scan public code repositories for credentials and API keys; revoke and rotate any exposed secrets immediately. Limit identity and application privileges : Apply least privilege to service accounts and applications, restrict user consent, and review permission or role changes. Secure cloud resources : Disable unnecessary public or anonymous access and review storage, identity, and secrets services for exposure. Detect post-compromise activity swiftly : Maintain endpoint and network detections for web shells, remote access tools, C2 traffic, and lateral movement; treat tool signatures as leads, not the sole detection method. Prepare for fast containment : Have procedures ready to revoke credentials and tokens, disable suspicious applications, and isolate affected systems. Coverage ARTEX is an orchestration framework that malicious actors can use to leverage extant offensive tools at scale and speed. Talos provides coverage for many of the most commonly observed tools we've seen deployed, including older ones such as Mimikatz, Cobalt Strike, and Acunetix. While an exhaustive list of coverage for these tools would be impractical given the length, please refer to this sample list of Snort and ClamAV coverage, which demonstrates some of the ways we would detect dual-use tooling associated with ARTEX. Talos will continue to monitor ARTEX-enabled attacks for novel tool deployment.
