title: Never be afraid to ask questions
summary: Amy reflects on a formative college anthropology course that taught her the power of asking questions to bridge cultural gaps. Welcome to this week's edition of the Threat Source newsletter. Back in college, I took an anthropology course called “Peoples and Cultures of Southeast Asia.” While the title sounded like your everyday anthro course, this one was a little different. It had fewer students, maybe around 10, and took place from 7 – 9 p.m., most college kids’ nightmare — but it was the perfect time of day to videochat with Malaysian students on the other side of the globe with a 12-hour time difference. My university had a 14-week semester, while the university in Kuala Lumpur had seven weeks, so our class had time before meeting the students to study Malaysia’s pre- and post-colonial history, political climate, and cultural and religious dynamics; watch famous Petronas Deepavali and Chinese New Year ads ; and (of course) drool over pictures of nasi lemak and teh tarik. When both classes began videochatting with one another (yeah, we used Zoom before it was cool), our questions were quite tame. This was partly because we were afraid of offending one another, and partly due to some thorny laws around political speech. They’d ask, “Where do you store your winter clothes during the summer? They’re so puffy!” or “How often do you eat at McDonald’s?” We’d ask, “What's your favorite food at pasar malams (night markets)?” and “How do you deal with the heat and humidity?” (The answer to that one: Malaysia, which is around the size of New Mexico, has around 1,000 shopping malls with heavenly air conditioning.) Over the weeks, with encouragement from our professors, a few brave souls from both countries began to open up about their opinions on the government, social justice movements, discrimination, and more. Their vulnerability was contagious and soon encouraged others to speak up more in class, and everyone began to ask more pointed questions. They’d ask, “What is it like to be openly LGBT+ in the U.S.?” We’d ask, “Do you think the new political party gaining the prime ministership will bring more change?” We soon developed a class motto: Never be afraid to ask questions. I firmly believe that questions asked in good faith create a space where it is safe to be curious, when everyone understands that the goal is understanding, not judgment. It’s perfectly fine to be honest about your lack of knowledge, and you’re always allowed to decline a question if the topic is too complex or personal to unpack in the moment. I'm grateful to still carry this philosophy with me today. I work with Talosians from around the world, where diverse backgrounds and communication styles can make it easy to misinterpret intentions. But assuming positive intent, asking questions, and being appreciative of the answers ensures that everyone is aligned, respected, and heard. To take a page out of Bill’s book (pun intended)... “I wish we could all live in a big house with lots of rooms, and windows, and doors, and none of them locked.” – Ursula K. Le Guin “I want to know why. Why everything. I don't know the answers, but a few days ago I didn't know there were questions.” – Terry Pratchett The one big thing Cisco Talos is breaking down a huge Microsoft Patch Tuesday release for November 2026, which addresses 1,095 vulnerabilities across various products. This month's massive update features 64 critical flaws, 48 of which could allow for remote code execution (RCE). Most notably, Microsoft warned that a spoofing flaw in Microsoft Office Outlook (CVE-2026-124194) is already being actively exploited in the wild. Additionally, don’t miss Google’s patch for a zero-day in Google Chrome’s XML component (CVE-2026-125350), released on Wednesday. The vulnerability is caused by a use-after-free memory management error that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code within Chrome's sandbox through a specially crafted HTML page. Google confirmed an exploit exists in-the-wild. Why do I care? When a Patch Tuesday drops with over 1,000 vulnerabilities, it is easy to feel overwhelmed. However, the sheer volume shouldn't distract from the handful of flaws that actually require immediate attention. Address the most realistic threats to your environment first to avoid burning out your team. So now what? Take a targeted, risk-based approach to this month's rollout. Start by addressing the actively exploited Outlook vulnerability (CVE-2026-124194), the Google Chrome vulnerability, and the critical RCEs in externally facing or core services like Exchange and Active Directory. title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
summary: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world's most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia. The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia. Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June). The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com. Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub . The head of Qilin goes by the handle “ Haise ,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise. The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP , a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44 . Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog]. The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com. Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations. The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk , which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals. IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure. Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket , Verified , and Zloy . Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru . The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru , the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation. Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia. Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521 , recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems. A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number + 79602347275 . Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru . IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites. That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014. More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane. Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful. Further reading: GangExposed , an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots. The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
summary: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month's Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws -- including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook -- and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla. Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe , Apple , Google and Mozilla . Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969. November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device. This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes. According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194 , a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office . Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS , macOS , watchOS and visionOS . Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined. Lee Neely , an instructor at the SANS Institute , noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18. “I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.” Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50 , which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350 , the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today ( Firefox 160 ) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity. Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited. Chris Goettl , vice president of product management at Ivanti , said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). “Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.” Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. title: Bring a tent, I've got the coffee: Lessons from it-sa
summary: Thorsten may have had to camp out in Nuremberg to attend it-sa, but the real story is the initiative to add a formal IT Security apprenticeship program in Germany for the thousands of young hackers ready to join our side. Welcome to this week's edition of the Threat Source newsletter. I'm just back from an interesting and demanding week of booth duty at it-sa Expo&Congress in Nuremberg, where Talos had a Point of Demonstration at the Cisco booth. I personally see it-sa as the German or European counterpart to the RSA Conference in San Francisco, with a slightly different center of gravity in at least two dimensions. First, the expo is the main event, not the congress. The congress is organized by associations, industry groups, and exhibitors, and plays more of a supporting role. title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
summary: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President ( AS2650 ). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period. The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica , a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications . Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge. There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer. Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight. Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network . “This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote . “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects. They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users. “Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.” All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation. As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
summary: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines. Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines. A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co. , a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “ XCPE ” (named after one of the malware’s core code components). The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group. The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year , residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects. “Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.” The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems . Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness). The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt , also known as Honeygain , which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs . In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source , which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut , a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies . In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut , saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM , Traffmonetizer , Jaguar , LINKFOG , BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode . Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient , a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks . Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users. Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets. In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology , concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components. The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com. Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass . In our November 2025 story, “ Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet? ” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker. That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee. Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linus Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links]. The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes. The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.” Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.” “The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.” Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals. “We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.” The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader. “As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.” Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

title: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer
summary: The self-deleting VOLTA infostealer steals credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets. Then, it uses LLMs to profile victims and rank their most valuable assets. VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value. If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails. This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator. There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort , is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage. After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token. The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets. Figure 1. The VOLTA-AUTODOXER workflow. The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.” VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models. Endpoint https[ :]// openrouter [ .]ai/ api /v1/chat/completions Default model anthropic/claude-opus-4.6 Fallback chain moonshotai /kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash Temperature 0.2 — deterministic, consistent output Request format Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0 Figure 2. Hardcoded model selection. Figure 3. Failover model selection to kimi-k2, and then gemini-2.5-flash. Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models. The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations. Figure 4. VOLTA's raw system prompt. The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped. Stealer capabilities VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report. Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to WlanGetProfileList and dumped to plaintext. Figure 5. VOLTA dumps plaintext passwords for every saved Wi-Fi network on the host. Figure 6. The organized collection targets. What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup. Figure 7. That’s right: Your Uber Eats history is now a potential liability. After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”. Figure 8. VOLTA’s exfil can happen in three stages: 1) after the stealer runs (“volta_log.zip”), 2) after the AI call (“volta_dox.zip”), (3) if the network enrichment produces anything (“volta_doxnet.zip”). The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated. Deployment model Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time. This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them. If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox. All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure. Countermeasures Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with --headless from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply. In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device. Conclusions VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in CLOSEDQUORUM , though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next. Figure 9. End-to-end VOLTA workflow. The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement. The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself. summary: In this edition of the Threat Source newsletter, William explores how PHP has taken over the conversation, Node.js has joined in, but underneath it all, there are still good people doing good work. Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter. “The darkest period of my life, so far, arrived the summer I was pregnant with my eldest son. The future was growing in me with all of its terrifying unpredictability, and I found myself anxious, unable to work and woefully at sea.” — Lauren Groff I doubt Lauren had this maniacal infosec news cycle in mind when she wrote about the terrifyingly unpredictable future, but honestly, she’s got our current careers down cold. Let he who is not woefully at sea cast the first water balloon? I’ll work on it. Here we are with PHP taking up every available ounce of oxygen, Node.js adding its own spice to the sauce... and here’s me, staring my screen blankly, waiting for an original thought to leak out and onto this page. Not to worry, none have. There is simply nothing novel to say because the entire internet has it covered. In triplicate. With graphs and compelling statistics and AI-generated evil bad guy images galore. These vulnerabilities are serious, and the remediations matter. Teams need to know what they run, find the affected systems, and get them patched and determine ways to secure systems that can’t be patched. I’m simply not going to add another dramatic headline to the stack or pretend there’s a clever new angle hiding in the margins. The thing I keep looping on is that the work underneath the headlines is familiar and it’s the real story. To defend your environment, you need a team that knows that environment, has enough time and expertise to investigate the telemetry, that can tell an anomaly from the usual benign noise, and take action. Yes, the right tools help, and without them you can’t do it — but the people doing the work are still what make those tools useful. Give smart people enough room to do smart people stuff. This is the entire ballgame. Read it again: Give smart people enough room to do smart people stuff. Because a good response starts way before the headline. Know what you own, who owns it, what version is running, whether it can be reached from the internet, what identities can do what task on the device, etc. When a fix is available, make sure it actually reaches the system you meant to fix. If a system cannot be updated yet, give that exception an owner and a deadline. Reduce its exposure, add monitoring, and keep checking until the fix is in place. “We’ll get to it” is not a plan. So, there may be nothing new to say about PHP this week, but the work is still worth talking about: Know your environment, take care of your team members, and keep paying attention when the weird thing stops being weird and starts becoming evidence. When the next headline arrives, help your teammate do the same. “The only thing that makes life possible is permanent, intolerable uncertainty: not knowing what comes next.” — Ursula K. Le Guin The one big thing Cisco Talos has recently discovered "NIK C2," a new command-and-control framework that integrates AI directly into its attack chain. This Go-based Windows implant allows adversaries to dump credentials, stream keystrokes, and deploy screen-locking ransomware. It also uses an integrated OpenAI model to analyze harvested data on the fly. By hijacking the victim's own API keys to fund these requests, NIK C2 collapses data collection and exploitation into a single, continuous session. Why do I care? By embedding a live AI pipeline directly into the C2 loop, NIK C2 turns a compromised host into an active operational asset rather than a passive foothold. Because it processes data and generates context-aware payloads locally, it erases the offline processing delays that historically gave defenders a critical detection window. Furthermore, by piggybacking on the victim's OpenAI account, threat actors completely mask their infrastructure, leaving no attributable trace and complicating incident response. So now what? Defenders must embrace continuous behavioral vigilance. Ensure endpoint solutions monitor for unusual local proxy routing, unexpected PowerShell executions, and unauthorized access to browser databases or crypto wallets.
